questions.q: What are the three things the `logging` module provides that scattered `print()` calls don't?
options: Faster execution, smaller memory footprint, and automatic parallelization
Severity levels for filtering, handlers controlling where output goes, and formatters controlling how each line is rendered (including timestamps)
Automatic translation into other languages, GUI output, and network streaming
Built-in encryption, compression, and automatic backups
questions.explain: logging adds levels (DEBUG/INFO/WARNING/ERROR/CRITICAL) for filtering by importance, handlers for choosing destinations (console, file), and formatters for consistent, timestamped output -- none of which print() provides.

questions.q: In the real example in this lesson, what did `logger.exception("backtest run failed")` produce in the console output?
options: Only the plain text message, with no other detail
An ERROR-level log line with the message plus the full current exception traceback, attached automatically
A silent log entry with no visible output
A prompt asking the user to confirm whether to continue
questions.explain: The real output showed an ERROR line followed by the complete Traceback, because logger.exception() called from inside an except block automatically includes the current exception's full traceback.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend `logger.info("...%d...", seed)` with placeholders instead of an f-string like `logger.info(f"...{seed}...")`?
options: Because f-strings are not valid Python syntax inside function calls

Because with placeholders, the string is only formatted if the log record actually passes the level filter, while an f-string is built every time the line executes regardless of whether it's filtered out
Because placeholders automatically encrypt the logged values
Because f-strings cannot contain integers
questions.explain: Lazy formatting means the %-style substitution only happens if logging's level filter decides the message will actually be emitted, avoiding wasted string-building work on filtered-out log calls -- a minor but easy-to-adopt performance habit.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the unifying rule for handling file paths, API keys, or environment-specific values in code?
options: Hardcode them directly in the script for simplicity

Never hardcode them into library or script code; read them from environment variables, .env files, or YAML/TOML config instead, so the same code runs correctly across machines without exposing secrets
Store them only in code comments
Always ask the user to type them in interactively at runtime
questions.explain: The lesson lists environment variables, .env files, and YAML/TOML config as the standard layers for this, specifically to avoid hardcoding paths or secrets that would break portability or leak sensitive values.

questions.q: How does this lesson connect logging and configuration back to the reproducibility theme from Chapter 2?
options: It argues reproducibility is impossible in Python and should not be attempted

It argues that logging the exact seed, resolved configuration values, and library versions used for a run -- as the real example did with seed, n_sims, and numpy.__version__ -- is what lets a research result actually be reproduced later
It claims logging has nothing to do with reproducibility
It states that reproducibility only matters for Monte Carlo simulations, not other research code
questions.explain: Chapter 2 established that a Monte Carlo result depends on the exact seed; this lesson extends that by showing that logging the seed, config, and library versions used for each run is what actually preserves the ability to reproduce a result months later.
